span: he cannot be successfully dispossessed by a true owner as the owner has lost his right, title and interest
why: Court's own reasoning that a person who has perfected title by adverse possession is protected against the true owner because the owner's title is extinguished.

span: mere possession, howsoever long it may be, does not necessarily mean that it is adverse to the true owner
why: Cites T. Anjanappa for the requirement of possession in denial of the owner's title; states the conditions rather than deciding the proposition, and adoption is not shown in this passage.

span: If the defendants are not sure who the true owner is, the question of them being in hostile possession as well as of denying the title of the true owner does not arise.
why: Court explains that adverse possession requires acknowledging another as owner and hostile possession, and that it fails if the claimant does not know the owner; the right is recognised but conditioned.

span: The question of adverse possession without admitting the title of the real owner is not tenable.
why: Headnote holding: the lessee's adverse possession claim fails for want of evidence of hostile possession known to the owner.

span: A plea of adverse possession is founded on the acceptance that ownership of the property vests in another against whom the claimant asserts a possession adverse to the title of the other.
why: Court explains the nature of the plea and says it must be assessed; the outcome appears in later paragraphs.

span: whether the plaintiff is entitled to a relief of permanent injunction against the true owner
why: Concerns an injunction by a plaintiff who has lost title, not acquisition of title by adverse possession.
